case_analysis.focal_point: Whether an ERISA plaintiff states a prohibited-transaction claim under § 1106(a)(1)(C) by alleging the existence of a plan-services contract with a party in interest, or must also plead that the services were unnecessary or the fees unreasonable in order to negate the § 1108(b)(2)(A) exemption at the motion-to-dismiss stage.
case_analysis.legal_provision: ERISA prohibited-transaction and exemption provisions: 29 U.S.C. § 1106(a)(1)(C) (prohibiting fiduciaries from causing the plan to furnish services between the plan and a party in interest) and 29 U.S.C. § 1108(b)(2)(A) (exempting necessary services contracts if compensation is reasonable); related definition of “party in interest” at 29 U.S.C. § 1002(14)(B).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue they pleaded every element of § 1106(a)(1)(C) by alleging that plan fiduciaries caused the plans to enter into service arrangements with plan service providers (who qualify as “parties in interest”). Under ordinary pleading and burden-allocation rules, they need not also plead around § 1108(b)(2)(A); rather, § 1108 is an affirmative exemption/defense on which defendants bear the burden (necessity and reasonable compensation). They contend the Second Circuit wrongly required plaintiffs to plausibly allege unreasonableness or lack of necessity to survive dismissal, effectively collapsing § 1106 and § 1108 and creating an acknowledged circuit split (with the Eighth and Ninth Circuits allowing claims to proceed on the § 1106 elements alone). They also argue the issue is purely legal, recurring, and this case is a clean vehicle because the prohibited-transaction claim was dismissed on the pleadings/finally resolved without factual development of exemptions.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that when a prohibited-transaction claim targets an arm’s-length contract for ordinary plan services (recordkeeping/administration, etc.), the claim is not plausibly unlawful unless the complaint alleges facts showing the contract falls outside § 1108(b)(2)(A)—i.e., that the services were unnecessary or that compensation was unreasonable. In their view, allowing plaintiffs to plead a prohibited transaction merely by alleging a services contract with a service provider would make routine plan operations presumptively illegal and turn § 1106 into a strict-liability weapon, inviting costly discovery and settlements. They thus defend the Second Circuit’s approach as a practical and text-sensitive way to harmonize § 1106 with § 1108 and to ensure plausibility under modern pleading standards, and they dispute that the split warrants review (or contend the Court should deny cert or consider another vehicle).
key_precedents: Nachman Corp. v. Pension Benefit Guar. Corp., 446 U.S. 359 (1980)
Dubin v. United States, 143 S. Ct. 1557 (2023)
Braden v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc., 588 F.3d 585 (8th Cir. 2009)
Bugielski v. AT&T Servs., Inc., 76 F.4th 894 (9th Cir. 2023)
Peters v. Aetna Inc., 2 F.4th 199 (4th Cir. 2021)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s overbreadth/workability concern is the strongest point for the respondent, but it does not justify converting § 1108(b)(2)(A)’s separately codified “shall not apply” exemption into an added pleading element of § 1106(a)(1)(C). As Justice Gorsuch notes (invoking Meacham) and Justice Kagan emphasizes (citing McKelvey/Dixon), our usual rule is that plaintiffs need not negate distinct statutory exceptions; nothing in ERISA’s text displaces that baseline at Rule 12. Harris Trust’s description of § 1106 as categorical prohibitions paired with § 1108 exemptions reinforces that Congress chose this architecture even if it creates litigation pressure. A narrow holding can still address Alito’s concern by recognizing defendants may raise § 1108 as an affirmative defense and, where the complaint itself establishes the exemption, courts may resolve it early without rewriting the statute’s elements.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—his workability concern that a literal reading makes routine service contracts “presumptively illegal” and invites coercive discovery—cannot justify importing § 1108(b)(2)(A)’s “necessary” and “reasonable compensation” conditions into § 1106(a)(1)(C)’s text. As the Chief Justice notes (citing McKelvey and Dixon), and as Justice Gorsuch emphasizes via Meacham, when Congress separately codifies an exemption using “shall not apply” language, the party invoking that exemption bears the burden; modern plausibility pleading does not authorize courts to reallocate that burden by rewriting the statute’s elements. If defendants believe the safe harbor is apparent from the complaint, they can raise § 1108 as an affirmative defense and seek dismissal, but that is different from requiring plaintiffs to negate the exemption at the threshold. On an originalist and textualist reading, ERISA’s prohibition-and-exemption architecture is a deliberate legislative choice, and policy discomfort with that choice is not a license for judicial revision.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas and the Chief Justice are right that § 1108(b)(2)(A) is framed as a separate “shall not apply” exemption, and McKelvey/Dixon reflect the general rule that plaintiffs need not plead around exceptions. But those cases do not require courts to treat a complaint that alleges only a commonplace service arrangement with a party-in-interest as plausibly alleging a prohibited transaction, when ERISA’s structure makes clear that Congress expected ordinary plan administration to proceed under the necessary/reasonable safe harbor and the practical consequence of the opposite reading is to make nearly every plan presumptively unlawful at Rule 12. Justice Sotomayor’s access-to-information point is serious, yet under Twombly/Iqbal a plaintiff must still allege enough factual matter to suggest the arrangement is outside the routine, lawful category—some indication of excessiveness, self-dealing, or unnecessary services—rather than relying on the statute’s breadth to trigger discovery. In my view, requiring that minimal, nonconclusory allegation does not “rewrite” § 1106; it enforces plausibility in a context where the literal elements otherwise sweep in virtually everything and invite precisely the coercive litigation dynamics Congress cannot have intended.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito is right to worry about coercive discovery and settlement pressure if routine service arrangements can be pleaded as prohibited transactions, but that practical concern cannot justify shifting the statutory burden to participants at Rule 12 when Congress separated the categorical bar in § 1106 from the “shall not apply” exemption in § 1108(b)(2)(A). As the Chief Justice stresses via McKelvey/Dixon, and as Justice Gorsuch underscores with Meacham, distinct exemptions are ordinarily matters for the defendant to invoke and prove; importing “necessary” and “reasonable compensation” into § 1106’s elements would effectively rewrite ERISA’s architecture and, in real-world terms, block access to information insiders control. Justice Kagan’s point that workability can be preserved by allowing § 1108 to be resolved on the pleadings when it clearly appears, or otherwise on a developed record, answers Alito’s threshold concern without immunizing conflicted arrangements. Given ERISA’s protective purpose and the asymmetry of information facing plan participants, I do not see a legitimate doctrinal basis to impose a heightened pleading requirement that Congress did not enact.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point remains the workability concern that bare § 1106(a)(1)(C) allegations could sweep in routine service contracts and create coercive discovery pressure, but that policy worry cannot justify importing § 1108(b)(2)(A)’s conditions into the prohibition’s elements when Congress drafted § 1108 as a separate “shall not apply” exemption. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes via McKelvey/Dixon, and as Justice Gorsuch notes with Meacham, the ordinary rule is that plaintiffs need not plead around distinct statutory exceptions; plausibility pleading does not authorize courts to reallocate those substantive burdens. Harris Trust’s description of categorical bars paired with exemptions reinforces that architecture and answers the “presumptively illegal” framing: the contract is prohibited unless and until the exemption is shown, and defendants can often test that defense early (even on the pleadings where the complaint supplies the facts). I therefore do not think Alito’s practical concerns, though real, undermine the textual-structural allocation Congress chose.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s workability concern—that routine service contracts will become “presumptively illegal” and trigger coercive discovery—deserves respect, but it cannot license us to reengineer ERISA’s elements at Rule 12. As the Chief Justice explains (citing McKelvey and Dixon), when Congress places a “shall not apply” carveout in a separately codified provision like § 1108(b)(2)(A), the ordinary rule is that a plaintiff need not negate it in the complaint; Meacham’s burden-allocation logic reinforces that the party seeking the exemption must raise and prove it. Alito’s proposed requirement that plaintiffs plead “unnecessary” or “unreasonable” effectively collapses § 1108 into § 1106, overriding the statutory structure Congress enacted and shifting burdens based on policy intuitions rather than text. Any overbreadth can be handled, as Justice Kagan notes, through treating § 1108 as an affirmative defense—sometimes resolvable on the pleadings when obvious, often on a developed record—without rewriting the prohibition.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s workability concern is the strongest point for Respondent—bare § 1106(a)(1)(C) allegations could sweep in routine service arrangements and create settlement pressure—but under the statutory structure Congress chose, that practical worry cannot justify collapsing § 1108(b)(2)(A)’s separately codified “shall not apply” exemption into a pleading element. As the Chief Justice notes (McKelvey/Dixon), and as Justice Gorsuch emphasizes (Meacham), distinct exceptions/exemptions are ordinarily for the defendant to invoke and prove; plausibility pleading does not authorize us to reallocate those substantive burdens by judicially adding “unnecessary” or “unreasonable” elements to § 1106. Harris Trust’s description of § 1106 as categorical prohibitions paired with exemptions reinforces that architecture and supports a narrow, institutionalist disposition: allow plaintiffs to plead the prohibition’s elements while preserving defendants’ ability to obtain early dismissal when the § 1108 defense is apparent on the face of the complaint. On my methodology, the remedy for overbroad litigation incentives lies in applying the exemption on an appropriate record and ordinary procedural tools, not in rewriting Congress’s scheme at Rule 12.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s workability concern—that a bare § 1106(a)(1)(C) allegation would make routine service contracts “presumptively illegal” and invite coercive settlements—deserves weight, but under a textualist approach it cannot justify importing § 1108(b)(2)(A)’s “necessary” and “reasonable compensation” conditions into the prohibition’s pleading elements. As the Chief Justice notes (relying on McKelvey and Dixon), the ordinary rule is that plaintiffs need not negate a separately codified exception, and Meacham, emphasized by Justice Gorsuch, reinforces that the party seeking the benefit of an exemption bears the burden to invoke and prove it. Alito’s invocation of modern plausibility pleading does not supply a license to rewrite substantive elements; Rule 12 can still dispose of cases where the exemption is apparent on the face of the complaint, but otherwise § 1108 is properly treated as an affirmative defense on a developed record. Harris Trust’s framing (as Justice Kagan and others mention) of § 1106 as categorical prohibitions paired with discrete exemptions confirms that Congress chose this architecture, and I do not see a doctrinal basis to invert it at the threshold.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that allowing a bare § 1106(a)(1)(C) allegation risks turning routine service contracts into presumptively unlawful conduct and enabling coercive discovery—raises a real workability concern, especially at the pleading stage. But as Chief Justice Roberts explains relying on McKelvey/Dixon, and as Justice Sotomayor and Justice Gorsuch echo via Gomez/Meacham, Congress wrote § 1108(b)(2)(A) as a separate “shall not apply” exemption, and our ordinary approach does not require plaintiffs to negate that exemption in the complaint. From a procedural-fairness perspective, importing “necessary services” and “reasonable compensation” into § 1106’s elements would effectively deny participants access to merits review where key facts are uniquely in defendants’ control, collapsing prohibition into safe harbor and weakening ERISA’s protective design. Alito’s practical concerns can be addressed through case management and by resolving § 1108 on the pleadings only when the complaint itself establishes the exemption, rather than rewriting the substantive pleading burden.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1106(a)(1)(C) sets out a broad prohibited-transaction rule (furnishing services between the plan and a party in interest), while § 1108(b)(2)(A) is a distinct exemption for necessary services on reasonable compensation; under the long-settled pleading and burden-allocation principle that a plaintiff need not negate a separate statutory exception, the exemption is properly raised and proved by the defendant. McKelvey v. United States, 260 U.S. 353, 357 (1922), reaffirmed in Dixon v. United States, 548 U.S. 1, 13–14 (2006), supports treating such separately stated exemptions as matters for the party invoking them, and requiring plaintiffs to plead unreasonableness or lack of necessity risks collapsing §§ 1106 and 1108 and undermining Congress’s chosen structure. A narrow holding that plaintiffs state a claim by pleading the § 1106 elements—while leaving defendants free to assert § 1108(b)(2)(A) on an appropriate record—better respects the statutory text and preserves predictable, precedent-based allocation of burdens, consistent with institutional legitimacy and restrained decisionmaking.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of § 1106(a)(1)(C) makes unlawful a fiduciary’s causing the plan to furnish services with a “party in interest,” and it contains no additional element requiring a plaintiff to plead that services were unnecessary or fees unreasonable. Section 1108(b)(2)(A) is written as a separate exemption—“[t]he prohibitions provided in section 1106… shall not apply”—and under the ordinary rule that a party claiming the benefit of an exception bears the burden, defendants must invoke and prove it rather than forcing plaintiffs to plead around it at the motion-to-dismiss stage. That allocation accords with this Court’s approach to statutory exceptions in separate clauses, see FTC v. Morton Salt Co., 334 U.S. 37, 44–45 (1948), and avoids rewriting § 1106 by importing § 1108’s conditions into the prohibition’s elements. Whatever policy concerns exist about routine service contracts are for Congress; our duty is to apply the statute’s original public meaning as enacted.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1106(a)(1)(C), read in isolation, sweeps broadly enough to cover routine, arm’s-length service contracts indispensable to plan administration, and Congress simultaneously enacted § 1108(b)(2)(A) to exempt precisely those "necessary" arrangements so long as compensation is "reasonable." At the pleading stage, a complaint that alleges only the existence of a services contract with a service provider (a "party in interest" under § 1002(14)(B)) does not plausibly allege unlawful conduct unless it includes facts suggesting the contract falls outside the § 1108(b)(2)(A) safe harbor—otherwise ordinary plan operations become presumptively illegal, with predictable, coercive discovery costs and settlements. While McKelvey v. United States, 260 U.S. 353 (1922), establishes the general rule that plaintiffs need not negate exceptions contained in distinct clauses, modern plausibility pleading and the structure/operation of ERISA’s prohibited-transaction regime support requiring some nonconclusory allegation of unreasonableness or lack of necessity to state a claim. That approach better harmonizes § 1106 with § 1108 and avoids converting § 1106 into a strict-liability weapon against routine service arrangements.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1106(a)(1)(C) states a categorical prohibition on a fiduciary causing a plan to “furnish[] … services” with a “party in interest,” 29 U.S.C. §§ 1106(a)(1)(C), 1002(14)(B), and § 1108(b)(2)(A) then supplies an exemption for “necessary” services with “reasonable” compensation—classic hallmarks of an affirmative defense rather than an additional element of the claim. Under the Court’s burden-allocation framework, plaintiffs ordinarily need not plead around statutory exemptions; the exemption is for defendants to invoke and prove, consistent with Gomez v. Toledo, 446 U.S. 635 (1980), and the general rule for “except as provided” provisos discussed in Dixon v. United States, 548 U.S. 1 (2006). Requiring dismissal unless plaintiffs plausibly allege unreasonableness or lack of necessity would collapse § 1106 into § 1108 at the pleading stage, undermining ERISA’s protective purpose and cutting off access to discovery for plan participants who lack inside information about fees and service arrangements. Practical consequences also favor petitioners: placing the pleading burden on participants would insulate conflicted transactions from review and disproportionately harm workers and retirees relying on fiduciary loyalty and transparency.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1106(a)(1)(C) sets out a straightforward prohibition: a fiduciary may not cause the plan to furnish services to a “party in interest,” and § 1002(14)(B) defines plan service providers as such parties—so a complaint plausibly states a claim by alleging that covered service contracts existed. Section 1108(b)(2)(A) is textually framed as an exemption for “necessary” services with “reasonable” compensation, and under ordinary burden-allocation principles a statutory exemption is for the party invoking it to prove, not an element the plaintiff must negate at the Rule 12(b)(6) stage (FTC v. Morton Salt Co.). Requiring plaintiffs to plead unreasonableness or lack of necessity to “negate” § 1108 at the outset risks collapsing the prohibition and exemption into a single pleading requirement, undermining ERISA’s careful statutory architecture and coherence (cf. Harris Trust; Conkright’s warning against atextual add-ons). Workability concerns about routine contracts can be handled through the exemption as an affirmative defense and through targeted pleading standards for factual allegations about fees, but not by rewriting § 1106’s elements.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1106(a)(1)(C) by its plain terms prohibits a fiduciary from causing a plan to “furnish … services” to a “party in interest,” and § 1002(14)(B) expressly makes plan service providers parties in interest, so alleging a services contract with such a provider pleads the statutory elements. Section 1108(b) is set out separately and states that “the prohibitions … shall not apply” to specified transactions, which under the familiar rule for statutory exceptions makes it an exemption/affirmative defense the defendant must invoke and prove rather than a negating element the plaintiff must plead around. Meacham v. Knolls Atomic Power Lab’y confirms that when Congress places exemptions apart from the prohibition, the party seeking the benefit of the exemption bears the burden, and nothing in ERISA’s text displaces that ordinary allocation at the motion-to-dismiss stage. Requiring plaintiffs to plead that services were unnecessary or fees unreasonable improperly collapses § 1106 and § 1108 and rewrites Congress’s chosen structure, raising separation-of-powers concerns by effectively adding atextual pleading elements.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1106(a)(1)(C) flatly prohibits a fiduciary from causing the plan to furnish services between the plan and a “party in interest,” and § 1002(14)(B) expressly sweeps in service providers; the complaint’s allegation of such a contract therefore pleads the statutory prohibition’s elements. Section 1108(b)(2)(A) is framed as an exemption for “necessary” services with “reasonable” compensation, and under ordinary burden-allocation principles—and this Court’s description of § 1106 as categorical prohibitions paired with separate exemptions—defendants bear the burden to invoke and prove an exemption rather than requiring plaintiffs to plead around it at the motion-to-dismiss stage. Harris Trust & Sav. Bank v. Salomon Smith Barney Inc., 530 U.S. 238, 241–42 (2000), treats § 1106 as categorical bars designed to prevent likely plan injury and recognizes § 1108 as a separate set of exemptions, which supports treating § 1108 as affirmative. Requiring plaintiffs to negate § 1108(b)(2)(A) in the complaint would effectively collapse the statutory structure and impose atextual pleading hurdles inconsistent with ERISA’s remedial design and traditional pleading rules.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of § 1106(a)(1)(C) prohibits a fiduciary from causing a plan to furnish services “between the plan and a party in interest,” and § 1002(14)(B) expressly defines plan service providers as “part[ies] in interest,” so alleging such a services arrangement pleads the elements of the prohibition. Section 1108(b)(2)(A) is codified separately as an exemption for “necessary” services with “reasonable” compensation; under ordinary pleading and burden-allocation principles, plaintiffs need not negate that exemption at the motion-to-dismiss stage, and defendants may invoke and prove it as an affirmative defense. That approach preserves the distinct textual roles of § 1106 (prohibition) and § 1108 (exemption) and accords with the general rule that a complaint need not anticipate defenses, as reflected in Gomez v. Toledo. Precedent from other circuits treating § 1108 exemptions as affirmative defenses (e.g., Allen v. GreatBanc Trust Co., reaffirmed in Albert) reinforces that allocation and avoids importing atextual heightened pleading requirements into § 1106(a)(1)(C).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1106(a)(1)(C) states a prohibition triggered by allegations that plan fiduciaries caused the plan to furnish services to a “party in interest,” and § 1108(b)(2)(A) is structured as a separate exemption (“shall not apply”) for necessary services with reasonable compensation—an arrangement that, under ordinary burden-allocation principles, places the burden on the party invoking the exemption. Consistent with Gomez v. Toledo, 446 U.S. 635 (1980), and this Court’s approach to statutory exemptions in Meacham v. Knolls Atomic Power Lab., 554 U.S. 84 (2008), plaintiffs need not plead facts negating § 1108 at the motion-to-dismiss stage when they have plausibly pleaded the elements of the § 1106 prohibited transaction. Requiring plaintiffs to plead “unnecessary services” or “unreasonable fees” upfront risks collapsing § 1106 into § 1108, undermining procedural fairness by shifting an exemption’s proof burden to plaintiffs before discovery and potentially insulating conflicted plan-service arrangements from meaningful review. That allocation also better aligns with ERISA’s trust-law roots, where a fiduciary (or the party benefiting from the transaction) must justify self-interested transactions as fair and reasonable under the governing standards.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether an ERISA plaintiff states a prohibited-transaction claim under § 1106(a)(1)(C) by alleging that plan fiduciaries caused the plan to enter a services arrangement with a party in interest, or whether the plaintiff must also plead that the services were unnecessary or the compensation unreasonable to negate ERISA’s § 1108(b)(2)(A) exemption at the pleading stage.
case_analysis.legal_provision: ERISA prohibited-transaction and exemption provisions: 29 U.S.C. § 1106(a)(1)(C) (prohibited transactions—furnishing of goods/services/facilities between the plan and a party in interest) and 29 U.S.C. § 1108(b)(2)(A) (exemption for necessary services at reasonable compensation); related definition of “party in interest,” 29 U.S.C. § 1002(14)(B).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that they pleaded every element of § 1106(a)(1)(C) by alleging that Cornell’s fiduciaries caused the plans to pay plan-service providers (recordkeeping/administrative vendors), which are “parties in interest,” for services—making the transactions presumptively prohibited under § 1106. They contend § 1108(b)(2)(A) is an affirmative defense (necessity/reasonableness) that respondents must raise and prove, not a pleading burden on plaintiffs. Petitioners emphasize a deep circuit split: in the Eighth and Ninth Circuits, their allegations would suffice; the Second Circuit nevertheless dismissed by effectively requiring plaintiffs to plead facts negating the exemption (unnecessary services or unreasonable fees). They also argue this case is an excellent vehicle because it was finally dismissed at the motion-to-dismiss stage and cleanly presents a purely legal, recurring question affecting large retirement plans.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that when a prohibited-transaction claim challenges ordinary, arm’s-length service contracts—ubiquitous in plan administration—the complaint must plausibly allege more than the mere existence of a services contract with a service provider. In their view, because § 1108(b)(2)(A) expressly allows necessary plan services for reasonable compensation, a plaintiff must plead facts supporting that the services were unnecessary and/or the compensation unreasonable; otherwise the claim would turn nearly every routine service relationship into automatic litigation. Respondents thus defend the Second Circuit’s approach as consistent with ERISA’s structure and practical administration, and suggest the case is not an ideal cert vehicle (including because petitioners’ other ERISA claims failed later in the case and because related petitions, such as Bugielski, may present alternative vehicles or broader issues).

Dubin v. United States, 143 S. Ct. 1557 (2023)
Braden v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc., 588 F.3d 585 (8th Cir. 2009)
Bugielski v. AT&T Servs., Inc., 76 F.4th 894 (9th Cir. 2023)
Peters (cited at 2 F.4th 199, pinpoint 244 in the briefs)
Sattar v. U.S. Dep’t of Homeland Sec., 669 F. App’x 1 (2d Cir. 2016)
Capital Records, LLC v. Vimeo, LLC, No. 09 cv 10101 (RA), 2018 WL 4659475 (S.D.N.Y. Sept. 7, 2018)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is administrability: because most plan service contracts are ordinary and often exempt under § 1108(b)(2)(A), he worries that treating § 1108 as an affirmative defense will trigger routine discovery. But as Justice Barrett and Justice Kavanaugh explain through McKelvey/Dixon, Congress’s choice to place the prohibition in § 1106 and the carveouts in a separate § 1108 that says the prohibitions “shall not apply” fits the default rule that plaintiffs need not plead around distinct statutory exceptions; Twombly/Iqbal polices factual sufficiency for the § 1106 elements, not by importing § 1108 into them. Meacham, invoked on both sides, reinforces that exemptions are typically for the party invoking them to establish and does not authorize us to recharacterize a separate exemption as a pleading element. A narrow holding can address Alito’s practical concern by emphasizing that dismissal remains proper when the complaint’s own allegations establish the § 1108 exemption and by reaffirming robust plausibility review of the § 1106 allegations themselves.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that the “except as provided in section 1108” clause and ERISA’s real-world contracting practices counsel requiring plaintiffs to plead facts showing “unnecessary” services or “unreasonable” compensation to satisfy Twombly/Iqbal. But as Justice Barrett explains via McKelvey/Dixon, when Congress places a prohibition in one section and then provides in a separate section that the “prohibitions … shall not apply” in specified circumstances, the ordinary rule treats that carveout as an exemption for the defendant to invoke, not an element the plaintiff must negate. Meacham, which the Chief Justice discusses, reinforces that exemptions are ordinarily borne by the party seeking their benefit; it does not authorize courts to transform a statutory exemption into a pleading requirement simply because many transactions may ultimately be exempt. The practical concern is addressed, as the Chief notes, by dismissal when the complaint itself pleads facts establishing the § 1108(b)(2)(A) exemption and by defendants’ ability to raise and prove the exemption promptly, not by rewriting § 1106’s elements contrary to the text’s original public meaning.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Barrett’s McKelvey/Dixon point seriously: § 1108(b)(2)(A) is phrased as a separate carveout (“shall not apply”), and that usually means the plaintiff need not negative it. But that default burden-allocation rule does not resolve the Rule 12 plausibility problem created by ERISA’s “except as provided in section 1108” cross-reference and the reality, emphasized in my earlier view, that routine plan-vendor contracting is ordinarily lawful rather than suspicious. As Meacham suggests, who bears the ultimate burden on an exemption can diverge from what must be alleged to render conduct plausibly unlawful; without some nonconclusory allegation of unnecessary services or unreasonable compensation, § 1106(a)(1)(C) becomes a near-automatic discovery gateway for ubiquitous arrangements. Justice Sotomayor’s reassurance that Twombly/Iqbal alone will screen fishing expeditions does not persuade me in this setting because the bare “party in interest + services” allegation will almost always be true and thus will almost always clear that minimal threshold absent a requirement to plead something that distinguishes wrongful from ordinary conduct.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is the practical one: absent a pleading requirement tied to “necessary services” and “reasonable compensation,” § 1106 could be used to pry open routine plan-vendor contracts through discovery. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett stress, Congress placed the prohibitions in § 1106 and the carveouts in § 1108 with classic exemption language (“shall not apply”), and under McKelvey/Dixon that separation ordinarily means the defendant bears the burden to invoke the exemption—not that courts may repackage it as an element at Rule 12. Twombly/Iqbal still does real work: plaintiffs must plausibly allege a § 1106 prohibited transaction (not just recite labels), and dismissal remains proper where the complaint itself pleads facts establishing the § 1108(b)(2)(A) safe harbor. On my pragmatic view attentive to access to justice, forcing workers to plead “unreasonableness” or “unnecessary” services before they can obtain information largely controlled by fiduciaries would functionally immunize conflicted arrangements and undercut ERISA’s protective design.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is his Twombly/Iqbal workability concern: that without pleading “unnecessary” or “unreasonable,” § 1106(a)(1)(C) becomes a near-automatic discovery trigger for routine vendor contracts. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett stress, the statute’s structure matters—§ 1108(b)(2)(A) says the prohibitions “shall not apply,” which reads like a classic exemption, and McKelvey/Dixon supply the default rule that plaintiffs need not negative distinct-clause exceptions at the pleading stage. Alito’s reliance on Meacham doesn’t move me because it distinguishes ultimate burdens from plausibility review, not judicially rewriting elements; we can address his practical concern through ordinary Rule 12 dismissal when the complaint itself pleads facts establishing the § 1108 exemption, and through early resolution once defendants invoke the exemption on an appropriate record. On pragmatic textualist terms, that approach best reconciles administrability with Congress’s chosen division between prohibition (§ 1106) and carveouts (§ 1108).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is the Twombly/Iqbal practicality concern that routine plan-service contracts could become easy pleading hooks, but that policy intuition cannot justify recasting a separately codified exemption into an element when § 1108(b) says the § 1106 prohibitions “shall not apply” in enumerated circumstances. As Justice Barrett explains (invoking McKelvey and Dixon), the longstanding default is that plaintiffs need not negative a distinct statutory exception in the complaint; plausibility review polices factual sufficiency as to the elements Congress actually wrote, not new ones we supply. Chief Justice Roberts is right that administrability is preserved because dismissal remains available when the complaint itself establishes the § 1108(b)(2)(A) conditions, and otherwise defendants can promptly raise and prove the exemption. Meacham supports allocating the burden of establishing exemptions to the party invoking them and does not authorize importing § 1108’s conditions into § 1106 at Rule 12 absent clear textual direction.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is the practical one: if § 1108(b)(2)(A) is treated purely as an affirmative defense, § 1106(a)(1)(C) could be wielded to generate routine litigation over ordinary plan-vendor contracts. But as the Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett explain, Twombly/Iqbal work can be done without rewriting the statute’s elements: dismissal remains available when the complaint’s own allegations establish the § 1108 exemption, and otherwise defendants can raise and prove the exemption on a prompt, appropriately limited record. McKelvey/Dixon’s default rule for distinct-clause exceptions fits ERISA’s structure here—§ 1106 states the categorical prohibition, and § 1108 separately provides the prohibitions “shall not apply”—and Meacham distinguishes ultimate burden allocation from plausibility without authorizing us to collapse § 1108 into § 1106 at the pleading stage. On an institutionalist approach, the narrower, text-respecting holding preserves administrability while avoiding a judicial reallocation of pleading burdens Congress did not clearly enact.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that, as a matter of plausibility, most plan–service-provider contracts are ordinary and generally lawful, so allowing a bare § 1106(a)(1)(C) allegation could invite costly discovery. But Twombly/Iqbal police factual sufficiency as to statutory elements; they do not authorize courts to reallocate what the statute treats as an exemption—especially where § 1108(b)(2)(A) is placed in a separate section and provides the prohibitions “shall not apply,” a structure that fits McKelvey/Dixon’s default rule (as Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize). Meacham, which Justice Alito invokes, distinguishes ultimate burden of proof from pleading, yet it confirms the baseline that the party seeking the benefit of an exemption bears it, and nothing in ERISA’s “except as provided in section 1108” cross-reference clearly converts § 1108’s conditions into § 1106 elements. Administrability concerns are addressed by dismissal when the complaint itself pleads facts establishing the exemption and by early adjudication of § 1108 on an appropriate record, rather than by rewriting § 1106 at the pleading stage.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—his Twombly/Iqbal workability concern that routine plan-vendor contracts would become a near-automatic discovery hook—raises a serious practical issue, but it cannot justify converting § 1108(b)(2)(A)’s separate “shall not apply” exemption into a plaintiff’s pleading element contrary to ERISA’s text and structure. As Justice Barrett (and Justice Kavanaugh) emphasize via McKelvey/Dixon, the default rule is that plaintiffs need not negate a distinct statutory exception, and Rule 12 already permits dismissal when the complaint itself pleads facts that establish the exemption. I also agree with the Chief Justice’s minimalist approach: require plausible allegations of the § 1106 elements, leave § 1108 to defendants unless it is apparent on the face of the complaint, which best preserves procedural fairness where the key “necessary/reasonable” facts are often in fiduciaries’ control. Meacham, as Roberts notes, supports allocating the burden of proving an exemption to the party invoking it and does not authorize reengineering pleading burdens to address policy concerns.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1106(a)(1)(C) sets out the prohibited transaction, while § 1108(b)(2)(A) separately provides that those prohibitions “shall not apply” to necessary services for reasonable compensation—classic exemption language that ordinarily functions as an affirmative defense rather than a pleading element. Under this Court’s approach to statutory exceptions in civil statutes, the party invoking the exemption bears the burden (and thus it need not be negated in the complaint), as reflected in Meacham v. Knolls Atomic Power Lab., 554 U.S. 84, 91 (2008). Requiring plaintiffs at the pleading stage to allege “unnecessary services” or “unreasonable compensation” to survive dismissal risks converting § 1108 into a heightened pleading rule not found in the text and undermines ERISA’s goal of uniform administration by producing divergent circuit pleading standards. A narrow ruling allocating the pleading burden to defendants preserves Twombly/Iqbal plausibility screening on the § 1106 elements while respecting Congress’s structural choice to place exemptions in § 1108.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of § 1106(a)(1)(C) categorically prohibits a fiduciary from causing the plan to furnish services to a “party in interest,” and petitioners plausibly alleged those elements, including that the vendors were parties in interest under § 1002(14)(B). Section 1108(b)(2)(A) is framed as an exemption—“[t]he prohibitions provided in section 1106 … shall not apply to”—which, as a matter of ordinary statutory structure and pleading practice, is not an additional element a plaintiff must negate at the complaint stage. Cook’s principle about exceptions being “ingredients of the offense” does not fit comfortably here because § 1106’s prohibition is complete on its face and § 1108 separately removes certain transactions from that otherwise-applicable ban. Nothing in ERISA’s text reallocates the pleading burden to plaintiffs to anticipate and negate § 1108(b)(2)(A), even if defendants ultimately bear the burden to prove the exemption’s applicability.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1106(a)(1)(C) cannot be read in isolation, because it expressly operates "except as provided in section 1108," and § 1108(b)(2)(A) squarely exempts the ordinary, ubiquitous plan-service arrangements at issue when the services are necessary and the compensation reasonable. As a practical matter, accepting petitioners’ view would convert nearly every routine recordkeeping/administrative contract with a "party in interest" (see 29 U.S.C. § 1002(14)(B)) into presumptive litigation on bare allegations, a result difficult to square with ERISA’s structure and real-world plan administration. Even if § 1108 exemptions often function like affirmative defenses, this Court has recognized that pleading standards can require a plaintiff to allege facts making liability plausible when the statutory scheme on its face indicates lawful and commonplace conduct (cf. Meacham v. Knolls Atomic Power Lab’ys, 554 U.S. 84, 91 (2008), distinguishing burden allocation from what must be plausibly alleged). The Second Circuit’s approach appropriately demands some plausible allegation of unnecessary services or unreasonable compensation to state a § 1106(a)(1)(C) claim in this context.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1106(a)(1)(C) on its face prohibits fiduciaries from causing a plan to furnish services to a “party in interest,” and Petitioners plausibly alleged that the plans paid recordkeeping/administrative vendors who fall within § 1002(14)(B), which is sufficient to state the elements of the prohibited-transaction claim at the pleading stage. The “necessary services”/“reasonable compensation” carveout in § 1108(b)(2)(A) operates as an exemption that functions like an affirmative defense, and requiring plaintiffs to plead around it improperly shifts information-forcing burdens onto participants who typically lack access to fee and contract details before discovery—an access-to-justice concern particularly acute for vulnerable workers dependent on retirement savings. Braden v. Wal-Mart Stores correctly treated § 1108(b)(2)(A) as a defense not required to be negated in the complaint, and the Ninth Circuit’s Bugielski approach reflects the same statutory structure; the Second Circuit’s heightened pleading rule would effectively insulate potentially conflicted service arrangements from scrutiny. While routine service contracts are common, Congress chose a prophylactic prohibited-transaction regime with broad remedial purposes, and courts can manage abusive litigation through ordinary plausibility and proof burdens rather than by rewriting pleading requirements.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1106(a)(1)(C) states a prohibition in categorical terms—fiduciaries may not cause the plan to furnish “services” to a “party in interest,” as defined in § 1002(14)(B)—and Petitioners plausibly allege those elements by alleging that the plans paid service providers for recordkeeping/administration. Section 1108(b)(2)(A) is framed as a separate statutory exemption for “necessary” services at “reasonable compensation,” and under this Court’s usual allocation rule for statutory exceptions, the party invoking the exemption bears the burden and it is not a plaintiff’s pleading obligation to negate it at Rule 12. This approach respects ERISA’s structure while preserving workability: defendants remain free to defeat routine service-contract suits by establishing the § 1108 exemption on a developed record, rather than converting an exemption into an extra element that rewrites § 1106 at the pleading stage. That reading aligns with this Court’s treatment of exceptions in civil statutes, including Morton Salt and Meacham, and avoids the Second Circuit’s effectively universal dismissal rule for § 1106 claims involving common service arrangements.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The statutory text draws a clear structural line: § 1106(a)(1)(C) states a prohibition, while § 1108(b) provides that “the prohibitions … shall not apply” to enumerated exemptions, including § 1108(b)(2)(A) for “necessary” services at “reasonable compensation.” Under the familiar rule that exceptions set out in a separate clause are matters of defense, the plaintiff need not plead facts negating the exemption; the party invoking the exception bears the burden to prove it. Meacham v. Knolls Atomic Power Lab., 554 U.S. 84 (2008), and McKelvey v. United States, 260 U.S. 353 (1922), reflect that principle, and the Second Circuit’s contrary pleading rule effectively rewrites ERISA by collapsing § 1108 into § 1106’s elements. At the pleading stage, alleging the plan furnished services to and paid a “party in interest” (as defined in § 1002(14)(B)) suffices to state a § 1106(a)(1)(C) claim, leaving § 1108(b)(2)(A) for defendants to raise and establish.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1106(a)(1)(C) states a categorical prohibition on furnishing services between a plan and a “party in interest,” and § 1108(b)(2)(A)’s “necessary services”/“reasonable compensation” carveout appears in a separate, distinct statutory section—so under the Court’s general rule, plaintiffs need not plead around that exception at the outset. McKelvey v. United States holds that a pleading invoking a general prohibition “need not negative” an exception set out in a “proviso or other distinct clause,” and Dixon v. United States reaffirms that allocation as a default rule; that approach fits ERISA’s structure with § 1106 listing prohibited transactions and § 1108 listing exemptions. Requiring plaintiffs to plead unreasonableness/unncessity would effectively convert the § 1108 exemption into an element of § 1106, contrary to the statutory design and to ordinary pleading practice for affirmative defenses. Practical concerns about routine service-provider contracts can be addressed through the defendant’s ability to raise and prove § 1108(b)(2)(A) at later stages rather than by rewriting the pleading burden.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text and structure of ERISA separate the prohibition in § 1106(a)(1)(C) (furnishing of services between the plan and a “party in interest,” § 1002(14)(B)) from the exemptions in § 1108(b)(2)(A), which permits “necessary” services for “reasonable compensation.” Under the settled pleading principle that a plaintiff need not negate an exception set out in a distinct statutory clause, § 1108(b)(2)(A) operates as an affirmative defense at the motion-to-dismiss stage, consistent with McKelvey v. United States, 260 U.S. 353 (1922), as reaffirmed in Dixon v. United States, 548 U.S. 1, 13–14 (2006). The Second Circuit’s approach effectively rewrites § 1106’s elements by importing § 1108’s conditions into the prohibition, contrary to the statutory text and the ordinary allocation of burdens for exemptions. Practical concerns about ubiquitous service contracts are better addressed through the defendant’s proof of the § 1108 exemption or through Rule 12 when the complaint itself establishes the exemption, not by imposing a categorical pleading burden to negate it.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1106(a)(1)(C) straightforwardly prohibits a fiduciary from causing a plan to furnish services to a “party in interest,” and once a complaint plausibly alleges those statutory elements, ERISA’s separate § 1108(b)(2)(A) carveout for “necessary” services at “reasonable compensation” operates as an exemption that the defendant must invoke and prove, not a pleading element the plaintiff must negate. That allocation accords with the ordinary rule that a party claiming the benefit of a statutory exception bears the burden, see FTC v. Morton Salt Co., 334 U.S. 37, 44–45 (1948), and with the fairness principle that plaintiffs need not plead facts “peculiarly within the knowledge of” fiduciaries and service providers, United States v. New York, N.H. & H.R. Co., 355 U.S. 253, 256 n.5 (1957). Requiring plaintiffs at the motion-to-dismiss stage to plead unreasonableness/unnnecessity risks insulating potentially conflicted transactions from review and undermines ERISA’s protective structure, particularly in the retirement-plan context where fee information and contracting details are often controlled by fiduciaries. Practical concerns about routine-service litigation are for Congress to address through the statutory text, not for courts to resolve by rewriting pleading burdens into § 1106’s elements.
